stops.name: Argel, the prophecies and the name of Abd-el-Kader
stops.campa: He collects, and sets down in order, the Muslim prophecies of the Mahdi circulating in Algeria: the man from Sus-el-Aksa who will destroy Orán, camp four months in the Mitidja, and level Algiers; the year 1264 of the Hegira; the ninety no exegete can explain. He warns his correspondent not to take it lightly with a modern Christian's scepticism — for unbelief does not yet exist among the Arabs, and the emir would not be so great a warrior if he did not believe. The desert chieftain is a religious fact.
stops.quote: La palabra incredulidad no existe todavía entre los árabes, i Abd-El-Kader no fuera tan grande guerrero, si no creyera i esperara firmemente.
stops.quote_source: Viajes, carta desde África, sobre las profecías árabes (enero de 1847)

stops.name: Argel, Marshal Bugeaud and the mounted infantry
stops.campa: The governor-general receives him and talks shop. Bugeaud calls his engagements batallas ambulantes and explains his plan to mount infantry on mules to chase the Arab horse into the desert; he is delighted to hear that in America, on the pampa, they have done exactly that against the montoneras. Both men agree on the rule: to beat a barbarous people you must stay civilised, or you merely parody them. Two continents' counter-insurgencies compare notes across a table in Algiers, and each recognises the other.
stops.quote: El mariscal comprendió mui bien que los franceses parodiarían a los gauchos árabes, i que para vencer a un pueblo bárbaro es preciso conservarse civilizado.
stops.quote_source: Viajes, carta desde África, entrevista con el mariscal Bugeaud (enero de 1847)

stops.name: The duar, the diffa, and the tents of Abraham
stops.campa: Provided with a burnous for the dignity of his office, he rides out with an escort to a camp of tents to be given the ritual meal. Approaching the thorn circle he is seized by vertigo: Rebecca and Jael seem about to step out of the doorways. Then he sits down, crosses his legs, gets cramp, notices his hosts sprawling at their ease, hauls one knee up under his chin the way a gaucho does — and the vision dies. He knows this place. He has been here his whole life.
stops.quote: ¡Tate! me dije para mí, yo conozco todo esto, i las tiendas patriarcales de los descendientes de Abrahan no están mas avanzadas que los toldos de nuestros salvajes de las Pampas.
stops.quote_source: Viajes, carta desde África, la diffa en el duar (enero de 1847)

stops.name: The plain of Eghris, the emir's father's house
stops.campa: General Arnault gallops him across the plain of Eghris outside Mascara. Here stands the paternal house of Abd-el-Kader, son of a great marabout to whom on pilgrimage at Mecca his son's destiny was revealed in a dream; here five thousand Arab horsemen gathered to proclaim him emir, in the manner, Sarmiento says, of Darius son of Hystaspes. He rides over the very field of the bay'a of 1832. That evening the general shows him a Revue des Deux Mondes and points at the title: Civilisation et Barbarie.
stops.quote: En aquella llanura está la casa paterna de Abd-El-Kader, hijo de un gran marabut, a quien en una peregrinación a la Meka le fueron revelados en sueños los altos destinos que estaban reservados a su hijo. Mas tarde en aquella misma llanura cinco mil jinetes árabes se reunieron para proclamar Emir a Abd-El-Kader.
stops.quote_source: Viajes, carta desde África, la llanura de Eghris cerca de Máscara (febrero de 1847)

stops.name: Mascara, the Arab trackers and the limit of the world
stops.campa: At the general's table the talk is of desert scouts, and Sarmiento sits up: the Arab baqueanos are identical to the ones on the pampa. They smell the earth to take a bearing, taste the roots of grasses, read the paths. He concedes that the Arabs outdo his gauchos — they talk across two leagues and scent cattle at three — and gamely defends the honour of the rastreadores of home. Beyond Mascara, he writes, European life stops; barbarism and the desert begin, and there his journey round the civilised world ends.
stops.quote: Entre otras cosas los baqueanos árabes me llamaron la atención por la singular identidad con los nuestros de la Pampa. Como estos, huelen la tierra para orientarse, gustan las raíces de las yerbas, reconocen los senderos.
stops.quote_source: Viajes, carta desde África, en casa del jeneral Arnault, Máscara (febrero de 1847)

stops.name: Rome, the ruins and the sculptors
stops.campa: The letter from Rome is dated the sixth of April, in the brief liberal springtime of Pius IX before the revolutions. He walks the Campagna, now desert or vineyard; he sits in Tenerani's studio among the first sculptors of Europe and notes, with an American's arithmetic, that they are taking orders from Boston. Rome teaches him what a ruin is worth and what it costs, and he leaves it, as he leaves all of Europe, admiring the monuments and refusing the model.

stops.name: New York, the drama without a plan
stops.campa: He lands from the Montezuma in September with almost no money and a fixed intention to dislike the place, and is overturned within weeks. The letter to Valentín Alsina that closes the Viajes is the hinge of his whole life: the United States, he writes, are a thing without any prior model, a kind of absurdity that shocks at first sight and frustrates expectation by fighting against received ideas. Everything Europe told him was impossible — a prosperous, literate, self-governing multitude — is here, running.
stops.quote: Los Estados Unidos son una cosa sin modelo anterior, una especie de disparate que choca a la primera vista, i frustra la espectación pugnando contra las ideas recibidas.
stops.quote_source: Viajes, carta a Valentín Alsina, Nueva York, 12 de noviembre de 1847

stops.name: West Newton, Massachusetts, the house of Horace Mann
stops.campa: He goes to Massachusetts to find the man whose Report of an Educational Tour he has read in Chile: Horace Mann, secretary of the state board, architect of the common school. Mann has no Spanish and Sarmiento no English, so Mary Peabody Mann sits between them and translates for hours. The common school — free, universal, tax-supported, coeval with the founding of a village — is the answer he has been looking for since a lottery in San Juan in 1821. The friendship with Mary will outlive her husband by thirty years and reach Paraná.
stops.quote: Un hombre no llega a la plenitud de su desenvolvimiento moral e inteligente sino por la educación: luego la sociedad debe completar al padre en la crianza de su hijo.
stops.quote_source: Viajes, carta a Valentín Alsina, Nueva York, 12 de noviembre de 1847

stops.name: Santiago, De la educación popular
stops.campa: Back in Chile he discharges the commission in a single enormous book: a comparative anatomy of the school systems of France, Prussia, Holland, Britain and the United States, with costs, statistics, buildings, salaries, methods and furniture, addressed to governments that do not yet exist. The title page lists him as first director of the Escuela Normal de Santiago. De la educación popular is the blueprint; twenty years later he will be president of a country and will build from it, page by page, without changing the plan.

stops.name: Santiago, Recuerdos de provincia and Argirópolis
stops.campa: In one year he writes the two books that make him a candidate. Argirópolis proposes a federal capital on Martín García island and a united states of the Plata; Recuerdos de provincia answers a slander campaign by telling the story of his own family — the loom, the fig tree, the friar uncle, the mother — and thereby invents Argentine autobiography. He is manufacturing a public man out of a poor provincial's life, deliberately and in print, at the moment when Rosas is about to fall and someone will have to be ready.

stops.name: Diamante, the Paraná crossed with the Ejército Grande
stops.campa: Urquiza rises against Rosas, and Sarmiento comes down from Chile to join him — as lieutenant-colonel, and above all as boletinero, keeping the army's press in a wagon so that the campaign will have a written account before it has a result. He crosses the Paraná at Diamante with twenty-four thousand men. He wears a French kepi and quarrels with everyone. The man who spent ten years arguing that the sword must serve the pen has arranged, characteristically, to carry both.

stops.name: Caseros, the victory and the quarrel
stops.campa: Rosas is destroyed in a morning on the plain by the Palomar de Caseros and rides away to a farm in Hampshire. Within days Sarmiento has broken with the victor: Urquiza is a caudillo too, a chieftain with a red band, and the boletinero says so in print and leaves for Chile in disgust to write Campaña en el Ejército Grande as an open letter of accusation. Twenty years of desired revolution, achieved and repudiated in a fortnight. He would rather be right than governing, until he is.
